[h3]Summary[/h3] The game is really good quality-wise, but I'm no longer the target demographic thus I can't recommend it. [h3]The good[/h3] The game has some really fun gameplay, fantastic scenary (it really feel like a theme-park ride) and breathe high quality in atmosphere, graphics, sound (cars, music and commentator) and it simply feels great to drive. [h3]The Bad[/h3] Starting the game you have to log into your MS-account, connect your accounts and connect to it whenever you start the game (I couldn't find a way to start the game without it). No big deal, but it was 5 minutes of direct annoyance and if my internet goes I can't boot the game. Playing for around 2 hours I got hit by 3 fullscreen splash screens that locked my game until I removed it, straight after a race, in-game, that tried to sell me the new game FH6, missing DLC etc. The in-game store is very noticable with "new notifications"-marks and it's part of the main menu. It felt like a mobile game in that regard. [h3]The Demographic[/h3] The game start with blasting off straight away, you get thrown into epic race scenes for about 5-10 minutes, which feel great, then you hit the character creation screen. It's a loud white and pink colored UI (which is the UI for the rest of the game). The first tab is to choose between very ethnically varied characters, next is genders including they/them... an two large tabs for choosing prosthetics and hearing aids... It's not a bad thing per se, but resources were spent on quite a lot of options that, to me, has no place in a racing game and is clearly catering to a certain crowd. After playing for 2 hours, I realized this was a theme. This game is very much trying to vibe with the "modern audiances" with bright colors and a chirpy attitude. I am not a fan of that. I wanted a simcade with muscle/super cars, high octane racing and a badass feel in a sleek upgraded package. I've realized I'm not the target demographic anymore, which is my issue and not the game being bad. However, it really pulls me out of the immersion. The Steam store pictures and trailers show none of this and all the focus is on cool cars going fast (in hindsight, the opening of the second trailer really hints at it). Thank god for Steam's refund policy.

Having done a 100% achievement run, this game can grow to be a little tedious at times due to its repetitiveness in terms of side content, but dive deep into the world and be BEING in Night City is something that is unforgettable. Add to that the Phantom Liberty expansion that adds a whole new area and quests to explore. Cyberpunk 2077 has become one of those games you keep thinking about even when you're not playing. The somewhat damaged quest however leaves a bad taste in my mouth. Why is the game a survival horror all of a sudden? It makes zero sense. Overall, if you like neon drenched cities and just driving around a city that feels alive. Nothing can beat this.

Elden Ring is one of those games that was elevated to fame even before its release. From Software, creators of the Dark Souls series, the game was billed as an extension of the familiar open-world formula. However, the end result is more complex. It's a game with many great ideas, but also with distinct design issues that often impact gameplay. Character Development System: One of the game's greatest strengths is the sheer variety of builds. Players can develop their characters in many ways, from the classic warrior with heavy weapons, through quick, arcade-based builds, to powerful magic-based characters. The development system offers significant freedom and encourages experimentation. However, the problem arises during gameplay. Quite often, a build that previously worked very well suddenly ceases to be effective. At some point, we hit a wall, and enemies or bosses become significantly more difficult for a given playstyle. As a result, instead of developing a character according to their own vision, the player begins to adapt to the demands of specific battles. Visuals and Game World: From an artistic perspective, the game looks excellent. The world is vast, diverse, and full of distinctive locations, and each region has its own unique atmosphere and visual identity. The world's history, co-created by George R. R. Martin, is also noteworthy. The lore is engaging and intriguing, though much of the plot remains hidden within item descriptions and dialogue fragments. For some, this is a key element in the world's mystery, while for others, it's a barrier to understanding the story. Camera Issues: The game's biggest flaw is the camera. This is where most frustrating situations arise. During combat, you can lock the camera onto a target. In theory, this is supposed to aid in tracking the opponent, but in practice, it often leads to chaos. The camera can get lost, suddenly change position, or be positioned at an awkward angle. As a result, the player cannot see enemy attacks, nor even their own character. The problem is particularly acute with large enemies. The camera can then position itself so close to the boss model that it's difficult to assess the situation on screen. Attempting to play without target lock also doesn't solve the problem, as the camera can still move on its own and doesn't always stay where the player intended it to be. In practice, this means that some deaths aren't due to player error or combat difficulty, but rather to technical and design issues. Repetitive Enemy and Boss Characters: Another drawback is the enemy design and the repetitive nature of many fights. In many places, the copy-and-paste method is evident. A boss, who we previously fought in a spectacular fight, later reappears as a regular enemy in a different location. This weakens the sense of uniqueness of the encounters and makes some moments less impactful. Battles can be spectacular, but that doesn't always mean they're well-designed. Some encounters feel heavily scripted. Sometimes, it feels as if they can only be completed sensibly with one specific playstyle, as other approaches are significantly more challenging. Approaching New Players: The game also disrespects players new to Souls games. At many points, it assumes the player already knows the mechanics characteristic of the genre. The game's systems are poorly explained, and many things have to be discovered through trial and error. The franchise's popularity is largely based on its reputation for exceptional difficulty. In practice, however, a significant portion of this difficulty stems from design issues. Unclear combat, camera issues, and inconsistent design decisions make the game challenging not because the enemies are well-designed, but because certain game elements make it difficult to play comfortably. The spawn point system is a good example of inconsistent design. Sometimes, a bonfire is located directly in front of the boss arena, with a statue allowing you to respawn even closer. In other situations, each death requires a long journey from the bonfire to the boss gate. With more difficult enemies, such as Malenia and the Blade of Miquella, this means that a significant portion of the time isn't devoted to the fight itself. Instead, the player runs back to the arena and reapplies buffs before the fight. As a result, up to a quarter of the time spent on a boss can simply consist of repeating the same path. Summary: Elden Ring is a game full of contrasts. On the one hand, it offers a beautiful world, interesting lore, and vast character building opportunities. On the other hand, it suffers from obvious design issues, such as camera work, repetitive enemies, and inconsistent combat design. It's not a bad game, but it's definitely not as flawless as some reviews suggest. Some players elevate it to a pedestal. This is mainly due to the reputation of the FromSoftware studio, and not necessarily due to the actual quality of all the game's elements. It's a title that manages to delight with its vision of the world, but at the same time, it can also be very frustrating at times.

I have played this game a lot, both with and without mods. I'll be blunt: it's a good game overall, but it has a lot of things dragging it down. Some say it's a 10/10 game, but I disagree. First of all, the biggest issue with this game, is input reading. Enemies and bosses don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. The enemy in Fort Gael is a good example: I try to shoot it with a crossbow, but it evade the moment I press the button, wether I'm aiming at it or not. This is dumb. -1 point. Next is wind-up attacks and tracking: a lot of bosses and enemies have ridiculous wind-ups that mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight. And if you try to reposition to avoid it completely, they will simply turn around 180 degrees and hit you with that attack anyway. This is cheap, not difficoult. -1 point. Then there is the game balance: it feels like they spent less than 10 minuttes to balance this game. In a lot of late game areas, enemies are just basic scrubs that do nothing, while a mid game area might have enemies that will utterly destroy you regardless of stats and defence. Bosses also do WAYYYY too much damage in proportion to how often they attack and how long their combos are. They get to kill me in 2-3 hits while being able to chain 3-7 attacks in a row, while I'm lucky to land 1 single hit before they jump away from me and just stare at me from the other side of the area. This is utterly stupid. -2 points. Next is the ability to respec, upgrade weapons, and change builds: this is hopeless.... the game is incredibly stingy with upgrade materials, and even if you obtain the bellbearings, the mats get increasingly expensive. You need a total of 12 of each basic smithingstone to max a weapon, from lvl 1 stones to lvl 9 stones. And lvl 8 stones cost 30 000 runes a piece, just to give an example. This discourages experimentation in a game with over 100 weapons. Respecing is also limited, as there is a fixed amount of larval tears you can obtain in a single playthrough. This can hardlock you to stick with the same build through the whole game. -2 points. Now we are down to 4/10. Now lets add the good things: The world is big, with lots of things to discover around every corner. Everything from weapons, mats and spells, to catacombs, castles and dungeons. Exploration is very rewarding. +2 points. Buildvariaty: if we look away from the horrible upgrade system, there is a lot of different ways to build your character. You can go pure meele, or pure spell/incantation builds, or heavily focus on status buildup, or make a combination of either of them, and much more. +1 point. Encounters: there are many npcs to stumble upon in this game, most of wich leads to new side quests or detours, or even new areas. Some are missable, wich can lead to missing out on certain questlines or items, but this isn't really a problem. The npcs of this game are fairly interesting, and some will even fight alongside you at certain bosses if you summon them. +1 point. Now we are at 8/10. There is a lot more that drag this game both up and down, but these are my takes. Personally I give the game a 7/10. It's an overall good game, especially with certain mods, but it can be really frustrating at times, and I can't really think of anyone I would ever recommend this game to. I had my fun, along with much frustration. Edit: Steam doesn't ask if the game is good, Steam ask if I would recommend it. I would not, unless it is with mods.
